question.text: How does mapping physical space onto a grid of numbers allow us to precisely partition paths, find balances, and safely navigate complex physical environments?

answers.answer: Giving every point a number (coordinate) lets us use formulas to measure distances, split segments in a ratio and find midpoints exactly.
solution: Each point gets a coordinate, so a position becomes a number.
The distance formula $AB=|b-a|$ gives exact lengths.
The division formulas give the exact point that splits a path in a ratio m:n (internally or externally).
The midpoint formula finds the balance point.
So paths can be partitioned precisely and checked by calculation.

checks.resolve_answer: Giving every point a numerical coordinate turns positions into numbers, so distances come from $|b-a|$, division points from the ratio formulas, and midpoints from averages. A path can be split exactly in a chosen ratio, and balance points or safe boundaries can be calculated precisely.

question.text: If we change the ratio of dividing a line segment, how will the position of the point on that line change? And how does thinking about ratios and reference distances help us understand locations in mathematics and in everyday life?

answers.answer: Changing the ratio m : n slides the point along the line of the segment; ratios and reference distances let us describe a location relative to known points.
solution: For an internal ratio m : n, the point lies on segment AB. A larger m compared with n puts it closer to B, and a smaller m puts it closer to A.
With ratio 1 : 1 the point is the midpoint.
For an external ratio, the point lies on the extension of AB, outside the segment.
Ratios and distances from reference points fix a position, for example on a map or when sharing a distance between two places.

checks.resolve_answer: Changing the ratio $m:n$ slides the dividing point along the segment. A larger $m$ moves it toward B, and a larger $n$ moves it toward A. Equal ratios $1:1$ give the midpoint. Internal ratios keep the point between A and B. External ratios put it outside the segment. Ratios and reference distances let us describe positions relative to known points. Examples are maps, dividing a road into parts, and placing objects at set fractions of a distance.
